Advanced Body Position and Bike/Body Separation

Performance outcome

The rider moves around a balanced, mobile position instead of holding one pose: the bike is free to move underneath them over compressions, roots, rocks, berms and steeps, while their mass stays calm, centred over the bike’s contact patches and ready for the next feature.

Who it’s for

Riders already comfortable on advanced (black) terrain who want to be smoother and faster, and racers whose video shows them being pushed around by the bike.

Before this lesson

  • Rides advanced terrain in control at their current pace.
  • Can stand, weight the pedals and move fore-aft on the bike without losing balance.
  • Has a coach or experienced rider available to film and review.

Why it matters

Almost every other skill in this curriculum (cornering, braking, pumping, rough terrain, jumping) depends on how freely the rider can move. Elite riders are not in a “correct” position more often; they have more range, and they choose where to be for each piece of trail.

Technical model

Position is a range, not a pose

A useful starting position is athletic and mobile: weight through the feet, joints bent with room to extend and compress in every direction. From there the rider moves forward, back, up, down and side to side as the trail asks. Universal cues like “always low” or “always back” fail because they remove that range.

Separating the bike from the body

Over a root or a compression the bike has to move: it rises, drops and pitches. If the rider is rigid, the whole system moves and the rider’s mass gets thrown around. If the arms and legs let the bike move underneath, the rider’s mass travels a smoother path and the tyres stay in contact with the ground.

Pressure, not just position

Where the rider’s weight goes through the bike decides which tyre has grip. Moving the hips forward or back changes how the load is shared between the wheels; driving through the feet or hands adds or removes pressure. The goal is to choose pressure on purpose, not to end up wherever the trail throws you.

Adapting to the terrain and the bike

Steep ground, flat corners, berms and jumps each ask for something different, and so do different bikes and setups. The same rider in good video will look different in each section, and that is the point.

Physics & maths

Centre of mass and base of support

The rider is most stable when their centre of mass sits over the base of support, the area between the tyres’ contact patches. On a slope, that base tilts with the ground but gravity still points straight down, so staying balanced means moving the hips relative to the bike. Bending the joints also lets the rider change height smoothly: the bike can travel a long way up and down while the rider’s centre of mass moves much less, which means smaller forces on the rider and more stable tyres.

A good Mathlete visual: trace the rider’s hip path and the bike’s path from the same video. The gap between the two lines is the bike/body separation.

Common errors

What you seePossible causesCorrection
Locked arms and legs: the bike and rider move as one block over bumps.Fear on the terrain, a position with no room left to absorb, fatigue, or speed beyond current skill.Coach to supply
Sitting far back on every descent, with a light, wandering front wheel.A learned “weight back” habit, steep-terrain nerves, or a bike setup that feels unstable.Coach to supply
Head and hips bouncing in time with the bike.Not enough separation; joints already fully bent or straight; too stiff a grip.Coach to supply
The same position everywhere, whatever the terrain.Position taught as a pose rather than a range; not looking ahead early enough to prepare.Coach to supply

Practice design

Setting
A short, familiar, coach-selected section that the rider can ride well below race pace, with a mix of compressions and small obstacles.
Focus
One thing per run: for example “let the bike rise into the hands” over a single root band. Keep speed constant so changes come from technique.
Feedback
Film from the side at a fixed, safe spot. Compare the rider’s description of the run with the footage before the coach comments.

Stop when

  • The rider is tired and quality drops.
  • Conditions change (wet roots, braking bumps developing).
  • Attention moves to speed instead of the focus.

Video analysis

What the rider and coach look for in footage:

  • Head and hips: how steady are they while the bike moves?
  • Range: does the rider use their arms and legs, or run out of movement?
  • Front-wheel pressure on the steep or braking sections.
  • Does position change appropriately between sections?
  • Repeatability across several runs, not one good one.

Ready to move on

  • Coach-observed: the rider adapts position to the terrain on a known section, run after run.
  • The rider can explain why their position changed in each section of their own video.

Educational checkpoints, not safety certificates.

Safety

Class 2: advanced riding skills. Needs the stated prerequisites, a controlled progression, suitable terrain and coaching guidance.

Practice only on terrain your coach has chosen, within your current skill, with the right protective equipment. Completing a lesson isn’t a safety certificate and doesn’t mean a rider is ready to try anything.
